---
title: "First Look at a Raster File: Dimensions, Bands, and NoData"
date: 2026-09-06
categories: [tool, raster, bilingual]
description: "Upload a GeoTIFF and get an instant summary — dimensions, resolution, band count, CRS, NoData, and per-band min/max/mean — in Python and R on the same map."
---

A vector file's first look answers "how many features, what shape, what
CRS." A raster's is a different set of numbers entirely: how big is the
grid, how many bands does each pixel carry, what does one pixel cover
on the ground, and which value means "no data here" rather than a real
measurement.

Get those wrong and everything downstream is wrong too — a slope
calculation that treats -9999 as a very steep cliff, a mean elevation
dragged down by a border of NoData pixels, a band mistaken for degrees
Celsius when it's really reflectance times 10,000.

Just want the summary, without the rest of the reading? Use the
[standalone tool](/tools/raster-inspector.html) — same engine, less
prose.

## 1. Upload your file

A single `.tif` or `.tiff` — no sidecars, unlike a shapefile.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

```

```{ojs}
uploadControl = WebGeoDS.Upload.createControl({
```


## 2. Why start with a summary?

Eight numbers, each answering a question that's otherwise easy to get
wrong by assumption:

- **Dimensions** — width × height in pixels. Determines how much work
  any pixel-by-pixel operation actually is, and whether a "small" file
  is small in bytes but enormous in pixel count (or the reverse).
- **Bands** — one grid of numbers, or several stacked together (RGB,
  a multispectral stack, a time series). Some checks and most
  visualizations only make sense once you know how many there are.
- **CRS** — same coordinate reference system concept as a vector file,
  same convention here: a missing CRS is assumed WGS84 and flagged,
  never silently treated as CRS-less.
- **Resolution** — the ground distance one pixel actually covers, in
  the file's own CRS units. A 30 (Landsat-scale) versus a 0.001
  (sub-meter) changes what questions the data can even answer.
- **Data type** — `uint8`, `int16`, `float32`, ... . The single most
  common source of a "why are all my values 0 or wildly wrong"
  surprise: an integer type storing values that were meant to be
  divided by a scale factor, or a float column silently truncated by
  being written back as an integer type.
- **NoData** — the sentinel value marking "no measurement here" (often
  `-9999`, `0`, or a type's max value) — as fundamental to a raster as
  a null is to a table column, and just as easy to accidentally treat
  as a real number if it isn't checked first.
- **Bounds** — the same bounding-box sanity check as a vector file:
  numbers wildly outside -180..180 / -90..90 are the CRS-mismatch tell,
  here too.
- **Value range** — the per-band min/max/mean, with NoData pixels
  correctly excluded. The fastest way to catch a unit mistake (a
  "temperature in Celsius" band whose values run from 200 to 320 is
  actually Kelvin) before it reaches an analysis.

```{ojs}
{
```

```{ojs}
    await sharedMap.fitToData(rInspect.footprint);
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Two cards side by side, same reasoning as the vector article: a
// combined "total pixel count" wouldn't mean anything, but seeing the
// two engines' numbers agree (or noticing where the CRS string or
// data type label doesn't) is itself the point — see section 5.
statCard = (label, s) => {
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.style.flex = "1";
  wrap.style.minWidth = "260px";

  const heading = document.createElement("div");
  heading.className = "webgeods-label";
  heading.textContent = label;
  wrap.appendChild(heading);

  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  wrap.appendChild(box);

  const row = (rowLabel, value) => {
    const dt = document.createElement("div");
    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = rowLabel;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };

  if (!s) {
    row("Dimensions", "—");
    return wrap;
  }

  const MAX_BANDS_SHOWN = 6;
  const bandLines = s.bandStats.slice(0, MAX_BANDS_SHOWN).map((b) =>
    b.min === null
      ? `Band ${b.band}: all NoData`
      : `Band ${b.band}: ${b.min} to ${b.max} (mean ${b.mean})`
  );
  if (s.bandStats.length > MAX_BANDS_SHOWN) {
    bandLines.push(`… and ${s.bandStats.length - MAX_BANDS_SHOWN} more band(s)`);
  }

  row("Dimensions", `${s.width} × ${s.height} px`);
  row("Bands", String(s.bandCount));
  row("CRS", s.crsWarning ? `${s.crs} ⚠️ ${s.crsWarning}` : s.crs);
  row("Resolution", s.resolution.join(" × "));
  row("Data type", s.dtype);
  row("NoData", s.nodata === null || s.nodata === undefined ? "None declared" : String(s.nodata));
  row("Bounds", s.bounds.join(", "));
  row("Value range", bandLines.join(" · "));

  return wrap;
}
```

## 4. Inspect: summarize your file

Run the same summary in Python or R on the current data (your file
uploaded above, or the built-in example below).

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #raster-inspect-py}
#| package: rasterio, numpy
import rasterio
from rasterio.transform import from_origin
from rasterio.io import MemoryFile
from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds
import numpy as np

path = None
for candidate in ["/uploaded.tif"]:
    try:
        with rasterio.open(candidate):
            path = candidate
            break
    except Exception:
        pass

# No file uploaded yet: a small synthetic hill built directly in
# memory (rasterio.io.MemoryFile — no virtual-filesystem path needed
# for a fallback), with one deliberately-NoData corner pixel so the
# NoData row below has something real to show.
memfile = None
if path is None:
    n = 20
    xs = np.arange(n)
    ys = np.arange(n)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
    elevation = (100 + 40 * np.exp(-((X - 10) ** 2 + (Y - 10) ** 2) / 30)).astype("float32")
    elevation[0, 0] = -9999
    transform = from_origin(12.40, 41.95, 0.005, 0.005)
    memfile = MemoryFile()
    with memfile.open(
        driver="GTiff", height=n, width=n, count=1,
        dtype="float32", crs="EPSG:4326", transform=transform, nodata=-9999
    ) as dst:
        dst.write(elevation, 1)
    path = memfile.name

with rasterio.open(path) as src:
    # Same convention as every vector tool on this site: a missing CRS
    # is assumed WGS84 with an explicit warning, never silently
    # treated as "no CRS" (which would make the footprint below
    # impossible to place on the map at all).
    crs_warning = None
    if src.crs is not None:
        crs_for_transform = src.crs
        crs_label = str(src.crs)
    else:
        crs_for_transform = "EPSG:4326"
        crs_label = "EPSG:4326"
        crs_warning = "No CRS found in the file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."

    # Per-band min/max/mean, NoData pixels excluded via masked=True —
    # a band that's entirely NoData reports nulls instead of a bogus
    # min/max computed from an empty array.
    band_stats = []
    for i in range(1, src.count + 1):
        band = src.read(i, masked=True)
        has_valid = band.count() > 0
        band_stats.append({
            "band": i,
            "min": round(float(band.min()), 4) if has_valid else None,
            "max": round(float(band.max()), 4) if has_valid else None,
            "mean": round(float(band.mean()), 4) if has_valid else None,
        })

    bounds = [round(float(b), 6) for b in src.bounds]
    try:
        wgs84_bounds = transform_bounds(crs_for_transform, "EPSG:4326", *src.bounds)
    except Exception:
        wgs84_bounds = src.bounds

    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = wgs84_bounds
    footprint = {
        "type": "FeatureCollection",
        "features": [{
            "type": "Feature",
            "properties": {"name": "raster footprint"},
            "geometry": {
                "type": "Polygon",
                "coordinates": [[[minx, miny], [maxx, miny], [maxx, maxy], [minx, maxy], [minx, miny]]]
            }
        }]
    }

    summary = {
        "width": src.width,
        "height": src.height,
        "bandCount": src.count,
        "crs": crs_label,
        "crsWarning": crs_warning,
        "nodata": src.nodata,
        "resolution": [round(float(r), 6) for r in src.res],
        "dtype": src.dtypes[0],
        "bounds": bounds,
        "bandStats": band_stats,
    }

if memfile is not None:
    memfile.close()

{
    "summary": summary,
    "footprint": footprint
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #raster-inspect-r}
#| package: stars, sf, jsonlite
library(stars)

path <- NULL
for (candidate in c("/uploaded.tif")) {
  ok <- tryCatch({ suppressWarnings(read_stars(candidate)); TRUE }, error = function(e) FALSE)
  if (ok) { path <- candidate; break }
}

if (is.null(path)) {
  # Same synthetic hill as the Python fallback — built directly as a
  # stars object via st_as_stars() on a plain matrix, with explicit
  # dimension metadata (offset/delta), rather than through a file: no
  # virtual filesystem needed for this side either.
  n <- 20
  xy <- expand.grid(x = 0:(n - 1), y = 0:(n - 1))
  elevation <- matrix(
    100 + 40 * exp(-((xy$x - 10)^2 + (xy$y - 10)^2) / 30),
    nrow = n, ncol = n
  )
  elevation[1, 1] <- NA
  dim(elevation) <- c(x = n, y = n)
  r <- st_as_stars(elevation)
  r <- st_set_dimensions(r, "x", offset = 12.40, delta = 0.005)
  r <- st_set_dimensions(r, "y", offset = 41.95, delta = -0.005)
  r <- st_set_crs(r, 4326)
} else {
  r <- read_stars(path)
}

d <- st_dimensions(r)
width <- unname(d[["x"]]$to - d[["x"]]$from + 1)
height <- unname(d[["y"]]$to - d[["y"]]$from + 1)
band_count <- if ("band" %in% names(d)) unname(d[["band"]]$to - d[["band"]]$from + 1) else 1

# Same missing-CRS convention as the Python side.
crs_warning <- NULL
if (is.na(sf::st_crs(r))) {
  r <- st_set_crs(r, 4326)
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
}
crs_label <- sf::st_crs(r)$input

res_x <- abs(d[["x"]]$delta)
res_y <- abs(d[["y"]]$delta)
bbox <- sf::st_bbox(r)

# read_stars() already substitutes the file's declared NoData value
# with NA at read time (verified: a -9999 sentinel pixel never
# pollutes min()/max() below) — but unlike rasterio, the sentinel
# itself isn't kept anywhere accessible afterwards. See section 5.
arr <- r[[1]]
band_stats <- list()
for (i in seq_len(band_count)) {
  vals <- if (band_count > 1) arr[, , i] else arr
  valid <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
  band_stats[[i]] <- list(
    band = jsonlite::unbox(i),
    min = if (length(valid) > 0) jsonlite::unbox(round(min(valid), 4)) else NULL,
    max = if (length(valid) > 0) jsonlite::unbox(round(max(valid), 4)) else NULL,
    mean = if (length(valid) > 0) jsonlite::unbox(round(mean(valid), 4)) else NULL
  )
}

# MapLibre/GeoJSON require WGS84 — the bounding box is reprojected via
# sf the same way the summary's own "bounds" field stays in the file's
# native CRS (same reasoning as the vector article).
bbox_poly <- sf::st_as_sfc(bbox)
bbox_wgs84 <- tryCatch(sf::st_transform(bbox_poly, 4326), error = function(e) bbox_poly)
fp <- sf::st_bbox(bbox_wgs84)

footprint <- list(
  type = jsonlite::unbox("FeatureCollection"),
  features = list(list(
    type = jsonlite::unbox("Feature"),
    properties = list(name = jsonlite::unbox("raster footprint")),
    geometry = list(
      type = jsonlite::unbox("Polygon"),
      coordinates = list(list(
        c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymin"]]), c(fp[["xmax"]], fp[["ymin"]]),
        c(fp[["xmax"]], fp[["ymax"]]), c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymax"]]),
        c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymin"]])
      ))
    )
  ))
)

summary_out <- list(
  width = jsonlite::unbox(width),
  height = jsonlite::unbox(height),
  bandCount = jsonlite::unbox(band_count),
  crs = jsonlite::unbox(crs_label),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning),
  nodata = NULL,
  resolution = c(round(res_x, 6), round(res_y, 6)),
  dtype = jsonlite::unbox(typeof(arr)),
  bounds = unname(round(as.numeric(bbox), 6)),
  bandStats = band_stats
)

# Round-tripped through JSON once more, whole-object — same reasoning
# as the vector article: R's atomic vectors don't cross the webR->JS
# bridge as plain JS arrays on their own the way a jsonlite-parsed
# list does.
result <- list(summary = summary_out, footprint = footprint)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

:::

## 5. Same spatial question, two languages

Python and R read the same file through the same underlying GDAL, but
the two engines disagree in ways a vector file's `sf`/GeoPandas split
never surfaces:

**Python** (rasterio)

```python
src.width, src.height     # dimensions
src.count                 # band count
src.crs                   # CRS
src.res                   # pixel resolution
src.dtypes[0]              # data type, as declared in the file
src.nodata                 # the NoData sentinel value itself
src.read(i, masked=True)  # one band, NoData pixels masked out
```

**R** (stars)

```r
st_dimensions(r)          # dimensions + band count
sf::st_crs(r)$input       # CRS
st_dimensions(r)$x$delta  # pixel resolution
typeof(r[[1]])            # R's storage type, not the file's declared type
# no direct equivalent — see below
r[[1]]                    # already has NoData pixels as NA
```

Three genuine divergences, not just naming differences:

- **CRS formatting** — same issue as the vector article's `st_crs()`
  vs GeoPandas footnote: `st_crs(r)$input` and `str(src.crs)` don't
  always print the same string for the same underlying
  CRS.[^raster-crs-format]
- **Data type** — `stars` always stores pixel values as R doubles
  internally; it doesn't expose the file's own declared GDAL type
  (`uint8`, `int16`, `float32`, ...) the way rasterio's `dtypes[0]`
  does. The R summary above reports `"double"` for *every* raster,
  regardless of what's actually on disk — a real limitation, not a
  rounding choice.
- **NoData retention** — `read_stars()` converts a file's declared
  NoData value to `NA` automatically at read time (confirmed: a
  `-9999` sentinel pixel never pollutes `min()`/`max()` above), but it
  doesn't keep the sentinel value itself accessible anywhere
  afterwards. rasterio does the opposite: `masked=True` excludes
  NoData pixels from a calculation, but `src.nodata` still tells you
  the raw number the file uses. That's why the R card's "NoData" row
  never shows anything but "None declared," even on a file that
  clearly has one — it isn't wrong, `stars` genuinely doesn't retain
  it this way.

[^raster-crs-format]: A GeoTIFF's own embedded CRS often resolves to a
human-readable name in GDAL's metadata (e.g. `"WGS 84"`), which R's
`st_crs()$input` reports directly — while an EPSG code assigned
explicitly in code (as the built-in example above does) round-trips
back as `"EPSG:4326"` on both sides. Worth checking which one you're
looking at before assuming a mismatch means an actual problem.

## 6. A raster with no declared CRS

The reusable cell pair above already builds a small synthetic hill
with one NoData pixel whenever nothing has been uploaded — click
**▶ Run** on both languages in section 4 to see it. This button swaps
in the same raster, minus the CRS, to see the warning row do its
job.[^raster-crs-missing]

[^raster-crs-missing]: An unreferenced raster isn't rare in practice —
a sensor's raw output, or a file exported by a tool that never wrote a
CRS tag at all. Nothing about the pixel *values* is wrong in that
case; only where they sit on the earth is unknown until someone
supplies it, which is exactly the situation the warning exists to
flag before a map silently plots it in the wrong place (or, for
`sf`/GeoPandas, refuses to reproject it at all).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
loadExampleButton = (label, pyCode, rCode) => {
  const button = document.createElement("button");
  button.textContent = label;
  button.onclick = async () => {
    await Promise.all([
      window.WebGeoDS.CodeCell.find("raster-inspect-py")?.setCode(pyCode),
      window.WebGeoDS.CodeCell.find("raster-inspect-r")?.setCode(rCode)
    ]);
    document.getElementById("raster-inspect-py")?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "center" });
  };
  return button;
}
```

```{ojs}
      type = jsonlite::unbox("Polygon"),
      coordinates = list(list(
        c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymin"]]), c(fp[["xmax"]], fp[["ymin"]]),
        c(fp[["xmax"]], fp[["ymax"]]), c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymax"]]),
        c(fp[["xmin"]], fp[["ymin"]])
      ))
    )
  ))
)

summary_out <- list(
  width = jsonlite::unbox(width), height = jsonlite::unbox(height), bandCount = jsonlite::unbox(1),
  crs = jsonlite::unbox(crs_label), crsWarning = jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning), nodata = NULL,
  resolution = c(round(res_x, 6), round(res_y, 6)), dtype = jsonlite::unbox(typeof(arr)),
  bounds = unname(round(as.numeric(bbox), 6)), bandStats = band_stats
)

result <- list(summary = summary_out, footprint = footprint)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)`
```

## 7. Where to next

A summary is a starting point:

- **Just needed the numbers?** The
  [standalone Raster Inspector](/tools/raster-inspector.html) has the
  same summary, no reading required.
- **Working with vector data instead?** Start with
  [First Look at a Geospatial File](geospatial-file-inspection.qmd) —
  the same idea, for GeoJSON and Shapefile.
- **Need to combine or transform bands** (an NDVI-style calculation, a
  reclassification)? A Calculator/Band Math tool is planned as the
  next tool in the Raster family.
